notes.meaning: Jesus explains that his return will not be hidden in a desert or whispered in a back room. Just as a flash of lightning instantly lights up the whole sky from east to west, his coming will be sudden, public, and seen by everyone. Believers do not need to chase after rumors of secret saviors, because no one will miss the real thing.

Jesus quotes a common proverb about birds of prey gathering over a fallen body. Just as vultures quickly and surely find a dead carcass, God's judgment will certainly arrive wherever there is spiritual death and corruption. Wherever sin makes people ripe for judgment, God will send the instruments of his justice.

differ.view: The Geneva Bible and John Calvin taught that the carcass represents Christ and the eagles are believers flocking swiftly to him as their only source of spiritual life.
Some dispensationalists view the carcass and birds of prey as a picture of severe judgment falling upon unbelievers at the second coming rather than the events of AD 70.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: John Chrysostom and other early church fathers saw the carcass as Christ's body in death, around which angels, martyrs, and believers gathering at the Lord's Table assemble.

notes.meaning: After the hard trials of history run their course, God will dramatically shake creation itself. Borrowing words from the Old Testament prophets, Jesus describes the darkening of the sun and moon and the falling of stars to show that earthly rulers and worldly powers are coming to an end. All created things must give way so God can establish his everlasting kingdom.

differ.view: John Wesley taught that Jesus begins speaking here of his final return, using 'immediately' from God's view of time, where a thousand years is like a single day.
Partial preterists teach that these cosmic signs represent the symbolic collapse of the Jewish nation and temple in AD 70 rather than changes in the physical sky.
Futurists believe literal disturbances in the sun, moon, and stars will occur right after a future seven-year tribulation period.

notes.meaning: The Son of Man will appear openly in the sky, wrapped in divine majesty and glory. Those who rejected him will mourn in deep sorrow and terror when they realize whom they opposed. For his faithful followers, this glorious sight brings comfort, because their King has arrived to set all things right.

differ.view: Partial preterists teach that Christ coming on the clouds was a spiritual coming in judgment in AD 70 to destroy Jerusalem and vindicate his claim as Messiah.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: John Chrysostom and early church tradition held that the sign in heaven will be the cross of Christ, shining brighter than the sun to convict those who rejected him.

notes.meaning: Jesus will send out his angels with a loud trumpet blast to gather all of God's chosen people. In ancient times, a trumpet called the whole assembly together, and here it signals the great reunion of the saints. Even though believers have been scattered to every corner of the earth or separated by death, not a single one will be forgotten.

differ.view: Dispensationalists teach that the angels gather believers who came to faith during a future tribulation, distinguishing this from an earlier gathering of the church.

notes.meaning: Jesus points to the fig tree as an easy lesson about noticing the signs of the times. When its branches grow tender and fresh leaves break out, everyone knows that summer is very close. Nature follows God's orderly seasons, and believers should pay attention in the same sensible way.

Just like the budding fig tree, the arrival of these events shows that the Lord is near, standing right at the doorway. God gives clear warnings in advance so his people will not be caught asleep. Recognizing these signs should move believers to live with patient hope.

Jesus promises that the events he warned about would begin unfolding before the generation alive in his day completely passed away. Within about forty years, Jerusalem and its sacred temple were destroyed by Roman armies, proving his warnings accurate. His words guaranteed that God's justice on the city was already at the door.

differ.view: Preterists teach that the entire prophecy through this verse found its complete fulfillment in the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 during the lifetime of the disciples.
Futurists teach that 'this generation' refers to the future group of people who will be alive to see the final end-time signs begin to take place.

notes.meaning: The physical universe seems ancient and steady, but one day even the sky and the earth will pass away. Christ's words, however, can never fail, wear out, or be broken. Believers can anchor their lives with complete confidence on what he has promised.

The exact date and hour of the final judgment remain a secret belonging only to the Father. Even the holy angels do not know it, and during his earthly ministry as a man, the Son did not make that day known. Since God has kept the timetable hidden, Christians should avoid guessing dates and focus instead on steady obedience.

Jesus warns that the world at his return will closely resemble the world right before Noah's flood. People back then had plenty of warning through Noah, but they refused to take God seriously. The final coming will catch an indifferent world completely off guard.

Before the flood, ordinary life continued as usual with eating, drinking, and weddings right up until the day Noah walked into the ark. Eating and marrying are not wrong, but people became so wrapped up in daily pleasures that they ignored eternity. They lived entirely for the present moment without any fear of God.

The ancient world refused to listen until the floodwaters rose and carried them all away to destruction. They did not truly believe the warnings until it was too late to escape. In the very same way, the coming of the Son of Man will overwhelm those who laughed at the promise of his return.

When the Lord arrives, a sudden and total separation will take place between people working side by side in the field. Outwardly they look the same and share the same labor, but God knows the difference between the righteous and the ungodly. One is taken into safety, while the other is left behind to face ruin.

differ.view: Pre-tribulation rapture teachers believe the one taken is a Christian caught up to heaven, while the one left behind must go through the tribulation.
Other futurists teach that the one taken is removed in judgment just as the wicked were swept away in Noah's flood, while the righteous are left to enter Christ's earthly kingdom.

notes.meaning: Two women will be doing common household work, turning a stone hand mill together to grind grain for bread. In a single second, the judgment separates them, taking one and leaving the other. Even the closest human partnerships cannot protect someone who has not made peace with God.

Because no one knows the day when the Lord will appear, Jesus commands his disciples to stay awake and keep watch. Keeping watch does not mean staying up all night, but living with an alert heart and a clean conscience. Faithful believers stay ready every day so their Master never catches them unprepared.

Jesus compares his coming to a thief who breaks into a house in the middle of the night. If a homeowner knew which three-hour watch of the night a robber was coming, he would stay awake and protect his belongings. Christians know the Lord is coming suddenly, so they must guard their souls with constant care.

Jesus directly applies the lesson of the thief by telling his followers to stay ready at all times. The Son of Man will arrive at a moment when people least expect him. Readiness is not something a person can rush into at the last minute; it is built through daily faith and prayer.

Jesus asks who among his followers will act like a trustworthy manager placed over a household. A wise steward remembers that the estate is not his own, and he faithfully provides food for the rest of the family on time. This describes leaders and believers who faithfully feed others with God's word and care for his church.

A servant is truly blessed when his master returns and finds him diligently carrying out his daily duties. The Lord does not look for big talk, but for steady faithfulness at our assigned tasks. Real honor belongs to those who persevere in doing good until the end.

The master rewards his dependable servant by placing him in charge of all his property. Great men in the ancient world promoted trusted household managers over entire estates, and Jesus promises an even greater reward in heaven. Those who prove faithful in small earthly responsibilities will share in the glories of Christ's kingdom.

A bad servant begins his downfall in his own heart by telling himself that his master is taking a very long time to return. Assuming that judgment is far away tempts people to become lazy and careless. When sinners think accountability has been postponed, they feel free to ignore God's commands.

Having put away a good conscience, the wicked manager abuses his power by beating his fellow servants and partying with drunkards. He acts like a tyrant over God's household while indulging his own worldly cravings. This pictures unfaithful church leaders who mistreat other Christians and adopt the sinful habits of the world.

The master will return on an ordinary day when the corrupt servant is not looking for him at all. Putting off thoughts of judgment does not delay the Lord's return by a single minute. The sudden arrival will turn the hypocrite's careless laughter into instant terror.

The master will cut the unfaithful servant to pieces and throw him out among the hypocrites. This severe punishment describes final judgment and being cast into hell, where there is only weeping and gnashing of teeth. Pretending to serve Christ while living for selfishness ends in bitter and endless regret.
